1121.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1121.hook: Parvati goes into the forest to win Shiva by her own austerity, and a young ascetic shows up to tell her she's wasting her life
1121.howItsDone: Hindus tell Parvati's tapas and her marriage to Shiva in the Shiva Purana and in poetry; some women keep fasts in her honor, such as Hartalika Teej, praying for a good marriage or for their husbands' welfare.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, spring came out of season, and Kama was burned to ash by the third eye: desire forced from outside couldn't win Shiva.

A princess takes off her jewels. She sets aside her silk and puts on bark. She leaves her father's palace for the mountains, a place where Shiva once sat, and begins. In the Shiva Purana, Parvati has seen what happened to Kama. Beauty didn't win Shiva; help from the gods didn't win him. So she'll do what Shiva himself does. She'll practice tapas. And one day, deep into it, a visitor comes up the path: a young ascetic with matted hair and a staff, who sits down and asks, very politely, what on earth she thinks she's doing.
screen: `JEWELS OFF, BARK ON.` → `SHE'LL DO WHAT SHIVA DOES.` → `A VISITOR COMES UP THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Tapas is austerity, disciplined effort that burns away what's easy and leaves what's strong. In the story, Parvati's tapas grows harder and harder. She stands in the cold, and sits among fires in the heat. She eats less, then less again, and tradition says she gave up even fallen leaves, which is why one of her names is Aparna. Her mother had begged her not to go. She keeps on. Then the visitor. He's courteous at first, then starts in on Shiva. Why this one? He smears himself with ash from cremation grounds. He wears snakes and rides a bull. Nobody knows his family. No house, no money, and he burned the god of love. A woman like you, he says, could marry anyone. Parvati's answer is the heart of the selection. She doesn't argue with the facts. She says, in effect, that the visitor doesn't know who Shiva is: what looks poor and strange from outside is exactly what she loves. And she won't sit and listen to him being insulted. She gets up to leave. Then the visitor drops the disguise. It's Shiva himself, who came to test her and found her immovable. Remember Sati, who would not hear her husband mocked. Parvati, born again, will not hear it either: the same loyalty, a second life. And where Kama's arrow failed, her own tapas succeeds. Shiva agrees to marry her. So the Shiva Purana's answer to yesterday is simple: what can't be forced from outside can be won by steady effort from within.
screen: `TAPAS: EFFORT THAT BURNS CLEAN.` · `SHE GAVE UP EVEN LEAVES.` · `THE VISITOR MOCKS SHIVA.` · `SHE WON'T LISTEN, AND IT'S HIM.` · then, large: `WON FROM WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to hold steady, your posture, your gaze or the breath, and when the mind wanders off, come back without scolding; that coming back is the effort. If a voice starts in, telling you this is pointless, notice it the way Parvati noticed the visitor, and stay put. If you pray, you can repeat Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as your steady point.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: Parvati's tapas, the visitor who mocked Shiva, and the loyalty that turned out to be the test.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Where the arrow failed, her steadiness didn't. See you tomorrow.

1122.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1122.hook: the wedding procession arrives at the mountain king's palace, and the bride's mother, watching from the roof, sees the groom
1122.howItsDone: The wedding of Shiva and Parvati is retold in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, and it is honored in temple festivals and in images of Shiva as Kalyanasundara, the bridegroom taking Parvati's hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, Parvati's tapas held, the mocking visitor turned out to be Shiva, and he agreed to marry her. Today, the wedding.

On the roof of the mountain king's palace, a mother waits to see her future son-in-law. Her name is Mena. Down the road comes the wedding procession, and it is splendid: gods in bright clothes, on fine mounts, with music. Each time a shining figure goes by, Mena asks, is that him? Is that Shiva? And each time she's told, no, that's one of his guests. Then the rest of the procession comes around the bend, and she gets her first look at the groom.
screen: `A MOTHER ON THE ROOF.` → `IS THAT HIM? NO, A GUEST.` → `THEN THE GROOM COMES INTO VIEW.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, Shiva's own companions, his ganas, come behind the gods. Some have strange faces, some are like ghosts and goblins, some are howling and dancing. In the middle rides Shiva on his bull, smeared with ash, snakes for ornaments, dressed like a man who lives in cremation grounds. Mena faints. When she comes to, she's furious. She blames the sage Narada, who encouraged the match, and says she'd rather see her daughter dead than married to that. She will not give her away. Parvati doesn't defend herself by pretending Shiva is ordinary. She simply says she will marry no one else. She has already chosen. The gods and sages plead with Mena. Then the story does something tender. Shiva, the god who burned Kama for trying to move him, bends for his mother-in-law. He takes on a form of great beauty, adorned like a bridegroom. Mena looks again, and this time she's delighted. The wedding goes ahead with music and rites, and the whole mountain celebrates. So who changed? Both of them, a little. Mena learns to look past the ash; Shiva lets the family see a face they can bear. Temple art remembers that second face: images of Shiva as the handsome bridegroom, taking Parvati's hand, are called Kalyanasundara, the beautiful one of the wedding. Mena saw the ash first. Parvati saw who he was. A good wedding needs both: someone willing to look again, and someone willing to show a gentler side.
screen: `THE GROOM: ASH, SNAKES, A BULL.` · `MENA FAINTS AND SAYS NO.` · `PARVATI: NO ONE ELSE.` · `SHIVA SHOWS A GENTLER FACE.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN. SHOW A GENTLER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose ways are strange to you, a new in-law, a coworker, a neighbor, and notice what you see first, the way Mena saw the ash. Then ask quietly what someone who loves them might see, and what gentler side of you someone else might need to see. If you pray, you can hold them before Shiva, or before God, in your own words.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: the wedding, a mother who fainted at the groom, a bride who chose no one else, and a god who showed a gentler face.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. A mother who looked again, and a god who let himself be seen. Until tomorrow.

1123.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1123.hook: three brothers ask for three flying cities that can fall to only one arrow, and the whole world becomes Shiva's chariot
1123.howItsDone: Shiva as Tripurantaka, the destroyer of the three cities, is retold in the Shiva Purana and shown in temple sculpture with his bow drawn; the story is recited and sung in Shaiva worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, a mother fainted at the groom, Parvati chose no one else, and Shiva showed a gentler face. Today, three cities.
screen: `LOOK AGAIN. SHOW A GENTLER SIDE.` · `TODAY: THREE CITIES.`

segments.voice: Every contract has a clause somebody hopes nobody will read. Three brothers in the Shiva Purana write theirs very carefully. They are the sons of Taraka, the demon whose boon sent the gods looking for a son of Shiva. With the marriage done, that son, Kartikeya, has defeated their father. Now the brothers practice tapas in the forest until Brahma, the creator, appears and offers a boon. They ask never to die. Brahma says no. So they ask for something cleverer.
screen: `THE SONS OF TARAKA.` → `NEVER TO DIE? NO.` → `SOMETHING CLEVERER.`

segments.voice: Three cities. Maya, the great builder of the demons, makes them: one of gold in the heavens, one of silver in the sky, one of iron on the earth. And here's the clause. The cities can be destroyed only when the three come into line, which happens rarely, and only by a single arrow. It sounds like never dying, with better paperwork. The brothers flourish, then turn on the gods, and the gods come to Shiva. Shiva needs a chariot, so the gods make one out of the world itself. The earth is the chariot, the sun and the moon its wheels. Brahma takes the reins. The Vedas are the horses. A mountain is the bow, and Vishnu himself becomes the arrow. When the three cities slide into line, Shiva looses the arrow, and all three burn at once. Some tellings say he barely needed it: he smiled, and the cities caught fire. That's why one of his names is Tripurantaka, the ender of the three cities. Two things stay. The brothers built their safety on a condition, and the condition was the crack: nothing built can be made un-endable, however careful the wording. And to meet that one moment, the whole world had to line up behind one arrow. On an ordinary Tuesday, a person can be three cities drifting apart: one part at work, one on the phone, one somewhere else. Once in a while, everything lines up, and a single act goes all the way through.
screen: `THREE CITIES: GOLD, SILVER, IRON.` · `ONLY ONE ARROW, ONLY WHEN THEY ALIGN.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD BECOMES THE CHARIOT.` · `TRIPURANTAKA, ENDER OF THE THREE CITIES.` · then, large: `WHEN EVERYTHING LINES UP, ONE ACT GOES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Notice where your attention is scattered: a bit in the body, a bit in something later, a bit in what already happened. Without scolding any of it, gather it piece by piece onto the breath, the way the three cities drift slowly into a row, and rest there, aimed and steady. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, as the breath goes out.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: three flying cities, one arrow, and a chariot made of the whole world. Shiva is Tripurantaka, ender of the three cities.

1124.title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
1124.hook: the creator's world won't grow, and the answer appears in a single figure: half Shiva, half the goddess
1124.howItsDone: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva as half man and half woman, appears in temple sculpture and bronzes and is worshiped as a picture of Shiva and Shakti inseparable; Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha opens by bowing to Parvati and Shiva joined like a word and its meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, three cities lined up and fell to one arrow, and the whole world was Shiva's chariot. Today, the last selection.
screen: `WHEN EVERYTHING LINES UP, ONE ACT GOES THROUGH.` · `THE LAST SELECTION.`

segments.voice: A bronze figure stands with a slight sway at the hip. On its right side: a man's flat chest, matted hair piled high, a snake for an earring. On the left: a woman's breast, smooth braided hair, a round earring, an anklet on the foot, the hip curving out. Not two figures standing close. One figure, split down the middle. This is Ardhanarishvara, and the Shiva Purana tells a story about why the creator needed to see it.
screen: `RIGHT SIDE: MATTED HAIR, A SNAKE.` → `LEFT SIDE: BRAID, EARRING, ANKLET.` → `ONE FIGURE, SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Brahma, the creator, has a problem. He makes beings from his own mind, and they don't multiply. The world stays small. So he does tapas, and Shiva appears to him in this form, half himself and half the goddess. Brahma bows and asks the goddess side for help. She gives a power of her own so that creation can go on, and in the story the world begins to grow through women and men together. So the picture isn't a riddle. It's an answer: creation doesn't go forward on one half. The name says it plainly: ardha, half, nari, woman, ishvara, lord. The lord who is half woman. Some Shaiva teachers put it this way: Shiva and Shakti, the god and his power, are never really two. One poet found an image for it. At the opening of his long poem the Raghuvamsha, Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined, he says, like a word and its meaning. Try separating those. A word with no meaning is noise; a meaning with no word can't be said. That's the last of the selections from the Shiva Purana, and it gathers up the rest: a pillar of fire no one could measure, Sati, who wouldn't hear her husband mocked, Kama burned by the third eye, Parvati's tapas and the visitor who was Shiva, a wedding where a mother learned to look again, three cities and one arrow. And now the two who were circling each other through all those stories, standing in one body.
screen: `BRAHMA'S WORLD WON'T GROW.` · `HALF SHIVA, HALF THE GODDESS.` · `LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` · `THE SELECTIONS, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `NEITHER HALF WORKS ALONE.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to the right side of the body, the hand, the shoulder, the foot, and breathe there a few breaths; then move to the left side and breathe there. Then let the line down the middle go soft, and feel the whole body breathing as one thing. If you pray, you can say the names Shiva and Shakti, or the name of God you use, and let them rest together.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection, and the last: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman, the answer when Brahma's world wouldn't grow.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Neither half works alone, and tomorrow, Shiva dances. That's the Shiva Purana, gathered up.

1125.title: Nataraja explained
1125.hook: a dancing Shiva stands at a physics lab in Switzerland, and the place to start reading him is the one part that isn't moving
1125.howItsDone: Images of Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of the dance, stand in many Shiva temples, especially in Tamil Nadu, where bronze Natarajas are bathed, dressed and carried out in festival processions.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the Shiva Purana with Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half the goddess. Now Shiva begins to dance.

Physicists walking to work at CERN, the particle physics laboratory near Geneva, pass a statue of Shiva dancing, a gift from India. Some of them stop. A god with four arms, one leg kicked high, hair flying out in streams, a ring of fire all around him, one foot pressing down on a small figure lying on its belly. It's a lot to take in on the way to the office. Over the coming days, i'll read him with you piece by piece. Today, where to start looking.
screen: `A DANCING SHIVA AT A PHYSICS LAB.` → `ARMS, FIRE, A RAISED LEG.` → `WHERE TO START LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First the name. Nata means dancer, raja means king: Nataraja is the king of dancers, Shiva as the lord of the dance. In the Tamil country of South India, bronze casters made images like this to be carried in temple processions. The inventory, quickly, since each piece gets its own day: a small drum in one upper hand, a flame in the other. A lower hand raised, palm out, the do-not-fear gesture from the mudras last year. Another lower hand swung across the body, pointing down at the lifted foot. One foot planted on a small figure. Hair flying out to the sides. A ring of fire framing it all. But the first thing worth seeing isn't on that list. It's the face. Everything else is in motion: the arms swing, the hair streams sideways as if he's spinning fast, the leg kicks across, the flames flicker. And in the middle of all that motion, the face is calm. Not straining, not grinning with effort. Still. Some images even give it the faintest smile. That's the key to reading the rest. The dance is often called the ananda tandava, the dance of bliss. Whatever this dance is doing, and it's doing a great deal, the dancer isn't frantic about it. The center is quiet. Think of a kitchen at dinner time, a shift with three people out sick, a child melting down in the grocery store: arms going everywhere. The picture suggests a face that doesn't have to follow the arms.

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your face: let the forehead go smooth, the jaw drop a little, the tongue rest, the eyes soften. Let the body move with the breath while the face stays quiet; if thoughts start spinning, let them spin like the dancer's hair, out at the edges. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, behind that quiet face.

segments.voice: A street vendor in Varanasi holds up a little drum shaped like an hourglass, two small heads joined at a narrow waist, two beads hanging on cords. He twists his wrist back and forth, and the beads fly out and strike the heads, left, right, left, right, a fast rattling rhythm that carries down the lane. It's called a damaru. Look up at Nataraja's upper right hand, and there it is, held between finger and thumb.
screen: `AN HOURGLASS DRUM, TWO BEADS.` → `A TWIST OF THE WRIST.` → `THE UPPER RIGHT HAND.`

segments.voice: The drum is tied to sound, and in this tradition sound comes close to the beginning of things. Before anything is made, something is said, or struck, or sung. So the drum in Nataraja's hand is read as the beat that starts the world, the rhythm the whole dance moves to. Grammarians tell a story about it. At the end of Shiva's dance, the story goes, he sounded the damaru, and out came the sounds of the Sanskrit language, set out in short lists. Those lists are real. They sit at the head of Panini's grammar of Sanskrit, and they're called the Maheshvara Sutras, the sutras of the great lord. The very first list begins with three vowels: a, i, u. Whatever you make of the story, notice what it claims: the ordered sounds of a language, the building blocks of hymns and grocery lists alike, came from the rhythm of a dance. Language begins as a beat. And a heartbeat is a small drum, a double knock, over and over, that started before you were born. A baby held against a chest is held against that drum. Footsteps are a drum. Rain on a roof. A kettle starting to tick as it heats. Long before anyone says a word to you in a day, something is already keeping time. Nataraja holds that beat up in his hand where everyone can see it. The dance starts here.
screen: `THE DRUM: THE BEAT THAT STARTS IT.` · `THE SOUNDS FROM SHIVA'S DRUM.` · `A, I, U: THE FIRST LIST.` · `A HEARTBEAT IS A SMALL DRUM.` · then, large: `LANGUAGE BEGINS AS A BEAT.`

segments.voice: Rest a hand on your chest, or two fingers on your wrist, or just listen inward, and find your heartbeat; don't count it, let it be the rhythm you sit to, and if it's hard to find, let the breath be your drum instead. Then listen outward to the sounds in the room, and let them join the rhythm too. If you pray, you can let Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, fall in time with the beat.
Nataraja explained. Today, the damaru, the small hourglass drum in his upper right hand: the beat that starts the dance, and in the grammarians' story, the source of the sounds of Sanskrit.
Your line: Nataraja explained. The small drum in his upper right hand starts the whole dance. See you tomorrow.

1127.title: Nataraja explained
1127.hook: a flame held in the open palm, level with the drum on the other side: the beginning in one hand, the ending in the other
1127.howItsDone: In Nataraja images the upper left hand holds a flame, read as dissolution, balanced against the drum of creation in the upper right; devotees offer lamps before Nataraja in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the drum: the beat that starts the dance, and in the grammarians' story, the sounds of a language. Today, the other hand, and the end of a week.
screen: `LANGUAGE BEGINS AS A BEAT.` · `TODAY: THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Birthday candles go out with a breath and a wish. A campfire burns down to embers while everyone's still talking. A match flares, does its one job, and is shaken out. Fire is the thing that's always ending. Now look at Nataraja. Opposite the drum, in his upper left hand, held up in an open palm the way someone might carry a small lamp, is a flame. Not a torch, not a weapon. Just fire, resting in the hand.
screen: `CANDLES, EMBERS, A MATCH.` → `FIRE IS ALWAYS ENDING.` → `A FLAME IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading of the image, the flame is dissolution. Things are made, they last a while, and in the end they're taken apart and drawn back in. The fire in that hand is the ending. Now look where the sculptor put it. Drum on one side, flame on the other, both raised to the same height, both held lightly, balanced across the shoulders like the two pans of a scale. The beginning in one hand, the ending in the other, neither higher, neither dropped. That's the picture's quiet argument. Read this way, ending isn't the enemy of the dance. It's half of it. The fire clears the stage so the drum can start again. And remember who's holding it: the one who dances in the cremation ground, smeared with ash, the groom whose looks made Mena faint. Ash is what fire leaves behind, and he wears it like clothing. Which brings us to the end of a week. It opened with Parvati's tapas and the visitor who turned out to be Shiva. Then the wedding, and a god who showed a gentler face. Three cities and one arrow. The lord who is half woman, and the close of the Shiva Purana. Then the dancer: the calm face, the drum, and now the flame. Every week ends. The flame in Nataraja's hand says that's not a failure of the week. It's how a new one gets room to start.
screen: `THE FLAME: THE ENDING.` · `DRUM AND FLAME AT THE SAME HEIGHT.` · `ENDING IS HALF THE DANCE.` · `A WEEK OF FIRE, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up: into the right palm put something that's beginning in your life, a friendship, a habit, a season, and into the left something that's ending, or needs to, a chapter, a role, a worry carried too long. Let both hands rest at the same height, and breathe with both, without lifting one or dropping the other. If you pray, you can offer both to Shiva, or to God, in your own words.
Nataraja explained. Today, the flame in his upper left hand: the ending, held level with the drum's beginning, both part of the same dance.
Your line: Nataraja explained. The beginning in one hand, the ending in the other. A week, kept.
